openingProblem.problem: Gorbachev came to power determined to save the Soviet economy. Six years later the shops were empty, prices were rising and the republics were taking over their own economies. Did perestroika fail because it went too far, or because it did not go far enough?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: was perestroika too radical or too cautious?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Why did Gorbachev start with the economy?
chunks.body:
When Gorbachev became General Secretary on 11 March 1985, Judt writes, he intended "from the outset" to devote his main efforts to overhauling the Soviet Union's moribund economy and the corrupt apparatus that ran it. The reasons were plain. The economy had hardly grown through the 1970s and was now shrinking. Oil was the main export, and as its price fell from its late-1970s peak, foreign debt climbed: $30.7 billion by 1986 and $54 billion by 1989.

His first slogan was "acceleration". The Library of Congress study notes that, despite Andropov's efforts to restore discipline, the system remained stagnant, and only when Gorbachev called for bolder change did acceleration give way to perestroika.

The most famous early measure was the **anti-alcohol campaign** of May 1985. Alcoholism was a real social disaster, linked to absenteeism, accidents and rising male mortality. Gorbachev limited the shops allowed to sell alcohol, closed distilleries, destroyed vineyards in Moldavia, Armenia and Georgia and banned restaurant sales before two in the afternoon. People called him the *mineral'nyi sekretar'*, the mineral-water secretary.

The campaign shows the early method well: a moral campaign from above, using the state's power to change behaviour. It also shows the trap. Alcohol was a huge source of state income: in 1979 the state took about 25.4 billion rubles in indirect taxes on it, more than it raised in income tax. Seventeen Moments explains that the campaign produced moonshine, organised crime and poisonings, and cut state revenue. The government covered the gap by printing money, which fuelled inflation, and the campaign was abandoned after 1987. This mattered because the first reform of the Gorbachev era weakened the budget, which meant that later reforms began with a larger money supply and a bigger deficit.

The early years, then, were not yet perestroika in the later sense. They were an attempt to make the old system work better, close to what Andropov had tried, and their failure pushed Gorbachev towards more radical change.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Gorbachev began with the economy because decline and debt threatened the state's power.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: He soon decided that the party itself was the obstacle, so the economy became a reason for political reform.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Early measures such as 'acceleration' and the anti-alcohol campaign tried to improve the old system, not replace it.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Alcoholism was a real problem, so the campaign was not merely economic.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The anti-alcohol campaign damaged the budget and fed inflation.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It may well have reduced drinking, so it was not a total failure.

useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant the government covered the gap by printing money, which fuelled inflation and left a larger deficit for later reforms.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the campaign addressed a real social disaster and may well have reduced drinking.

chunks.title: Perestroika: reform from above, 1986–1988
chunks.body:
Only in early 1987, the Library of Congress study notes, did perestroika become "a full-scale campaign". At the Central Committee plenum of January 1987 Gorbachev applied the label to his programme of devolving economic and political control. In economics it meant three things: more freedom for plant managers, some individual initiative, and the chance to make a profit.

The first step was cautious. The **Law on Individual Labour Activity** of 19 November 1986 allowed private work, but only "based exclusively on the personal labor of citizens and members of their families". Judt notes how few took up the offer: three years later there were just 300,000 businesspeople in a population of 290 million. Decrees from early 1987, consolidated in the **Law on Cooperatives** of 26 May 1988, went further, putting profit-making cooperatives on the same footing as state enterprises. By the end of 1987 about 150,000 people worked in 13,921 new cooperatives, and their restaurants, hairdressers and repair shops gave better service than the state.

The central reform was the **Law on State Enterprise**, which came into effect in January 1988 and let enterprises set many of their own prices and wages. The idea was to make managers respond to demand rather than to Gosplan's orders.

Judt explains why this was so hard. Reform faced a "chicken-egg dilemma": if enterprises were freed before a market existed, they had no prices to guide them, so there would be more shortages, not fewer, as everyone fell back on regional self-sufficiency and barter. But a market could not simply be announced. The word "capitalism" had been abhorred for decades, and Gorbachev avoided any mention of a market economy until late 1987, and then spoke only of a "socialist market". The compromise was to build model enterprises from above, supplied with materials and labour. They worked only with heavy subsidies, starving other enterprises, and managers, unsure whether the old controls would return, stockpiled whatever they could.

This mattered because perestroika in 1986–1988 was still reform by decree: it loosened controls without creating the prices, property rights and competition that a market needs, which meant that the old system was weakened before a new one existed. Robert Campbell's verdict is blunt: the enterprise law and the cooperatives "basically involved tinkering with details".

argumentsThatWork.claim: Perestroika in 1986–1988 was reform from above: it loosened controls but kept planning, state ownership and fixed prices.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The cooperatives were a real step towards private enterprise.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The cooperatives showed what initiative could do, but they were small and resented.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Their productivity was higher than in state enterprises, so the problem was scale and context, not the idea.

chunks.title: Why did reform make things worse?
chunks.body:
By 1988 the results of perestroika were the opposite of what Gorbachev intended. The Library of Congress study traces the chain. Once enterprises could set wages, workers demanded steep increases. The government paid by printing money. With more money chasing goods sold at fixed prices in state shops, those goods "quickly disappeared as speculators snatched them up or producers ceased making deliveries". By September 1988 many staple products could not be found even in Moscow.

The cooperatives made matters worse in the public mind. Seventeen Moments records that citizens deluged the press with letters complaining about their high prices, about cooperatives taking the best workers from state enterprises, and about their use of state supplies, which deepened the shortages. Local officials taxed them heavily and criminals ran protection rackets. *Kooperativshchiki* became a term of abuse. A reform meant to show the benefits of initiative instead linked private enterprise with profiteering and crime.

Gorbachev's response was to push harder against the party machine. During 1988–89 he ordered regional party committees to stop interfering in the economy and cut the staffs of the economic ministries. But nothing replaced them. In the study's words, "without the state and the party to hold it together and guide it, the economy went into free-fall". By 1990, Seventeen Moments notes, enterprises settled accounts by barter, regions embargoed shipments to their neighbours, and citizens queued with ration coupons for sugar, tea and soap.

Judt explains why this outcome was built into the reform. Serious economic reform meant relaxing or abandoning controls, which first made the problems worse, and it meant "just what it said: a loss of control. But Communism depended upon control—indeed Communism *was* control." Gorbachev concluded that to reform the economy the party would first have to reform itself. This mattered because it turned an economic programme into a political one, which meant that glasnost and democratisation, not prices, became the centre of his project. Archie Brown's judgement is that perestroika's aim of injecting new dynamism into the economy failed, while democratisation came to be given a higher priority than economic reform.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Partial reform produced inflation and shortage: wage freedom plus fixed prices emptied the shops.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Shortages were endemic before 1985, so reform worsened rather than created them.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Removing the party from the economy without a market left nothing to coordinate it.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The republics' own actions after 1990 also broke supply chains, so not all the chaos came from Moscow's reforms.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The economic failure pushed Gorbachev towards political reform.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Brown suggests his goals evolved anyway, so political reform was a choice, not only a response.

useItInAnEssay.judge: The law was therefore a major cause of the crisis of 1988–1991, but as an accelerant rather than the origin.

chunks.title: 1990–1991: the war of programmes
chunks.body:
By 1990, Seventeen Moments argues, the question "was no longer whether the Soviet Union would move to a market but who would be holding the property when it got there". Three programmes competed, in what contemporaries called the "war of programmes".

The government moved first. On 24 May 1990 Prime Minister Nikolai Ryzhkov proposed a regulated market reached in stages, with the state keeping major industry. His honesty about prices destroyed the plan: the announcement that bread would cost about three times more from July emptied the shops within days, and deputies sent the programme back.

The radical alternative came from outside the government. On 27 July Gorbachev and Boris Yeltsin, chairman of the Russian parliament, jointly commissioned a team under the economist Stanislav Shatalin. Its programme, issued on 1 September as *Transition to the Market* and soon called the **500 Days Plan**, accepted private property, market prices, enterprise independence and an open economy, with a timetable. One of its most radical features was federal: sovereignty over resources and taxes would pass to the republics. The Russian Supreme Soviet adopted it on 11 September. The Union parliament did not. Instead it gave Gorbachev powers to rule by decree, and on 18 October a compromise, the "Basic Guidelines", kept the plan's stages but dropped its timetable. Grigorii Yavlinsky, whose earlier "400 Days" scheme the plan built on, resigned from the Russian government, saying that a hedgehog cannot be crossed with a grass snake.

Why did Gorbachev retreat? Robert Campbell argues that the plan's acceptance of the republics' economic independence was "fatal", because Gorbachev "was not ready to accept a diminution of central power". Seventeen Moments reaches the same conclusion: the compromise was in fact "a decision that the union would keep the union's property".

What followed was confiscation, not reform. In January 1991 Gorbachev replaced Ryzhkov with Valentin Pavlov, who withdrew 50- and 100-ruble notes from circulation at short notice, causing panic and deep mistrust, and raised prices in April. Coal miners struck from March to May against inflation that had wiped out their wage gains, demanding Gorbachev's resignation and the transfer of mines to the republics. Gorbachev had to ask the West for financial aid. This mattered because the centre lost the economic argument to the republics, which meant that economic failure became a cause of the Union's political collapse.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: He also feared the social cost of rapid price rises, as Ryzhkov's bread plan had shown.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The centre's economic failure in 1990–1991 shifted authority to the republics.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The republics' nationalism had political roots that did not depend on economics.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Pavlov's measures showed that the state's remaining tool was confiscation, which destroyed trust.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Inflation was so severe that some monetary measure was unavoidable.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent did perestroika fail to achieve its economic aims between 1985 and 1991?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far, using degree language
decodeKey.judgement: How far perestroika failed, measured against its aims as they changed

modelPlan.thesis: Perestroika largely failed in its economic aims, because it loosened planning without creating a market; but its aims changed, and by 1990 the decisive obstacle was Gorbachev's refusal to give the republics economic power.

arguments.claim: Perestroika's partial reforms produced shortage and inflation (named factor first).
Early measures weakened the budget before perestroika proper began.
The cooperatives were a limited success, but small and resented.
In 1990–1991 the centre rejected the market and turned to confiscation.

modelPlan.counter: Brown argues that Gorbachev's aims changed and democratisation became his priority, so judging him by economic aims alone is unfair.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did the economy grow, as the original aim required? No: it shrank and debt rose, so the failure is clear, however the aims changed.

segments.text: Perestroika largely failed to achieve its economic aims, because it weakened central planning before it created a market.
The Law on State Enterprise let enterprises set wages from January 1988, and by September 1988 many staples could not be found even in Moscow.
This meant that wages rose while prices stayed fixed, so the government printed money and goods disappeared from state shops.
However, Archie Brown argues that Gorbachev's aims evolved, and that democratisation came to matter more to him than economic reform.
Judged by its original aim of reviving the economy, perestroika therefore failed, even if its political aims went further.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Gorbachev's economic reforms made the Soviet economy worse, not better.” Discuss with reference to the period 1985 to 1991.
essayQuestions.scope: Soviet Union; effects of economic reform

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim for and against, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim that the reforms made things worse
decodeKey.judgement: How far the reforms, rather than inherited problems, caused the decline

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is largely right: the reforms turned stagnation into shortage and inflation; but the inherited problems were real, and the most damaging choices of 1990–1991 were refusals to reform rather than reforms.

arguments.claim: For: the anti-alcohol campaign and money printing fed inflation.
For: the enterprise law and the withdrawal of the party produced shortage and free fall.
Against: the economy was already shrinking when Gorbachev took over.
Against: the damage of 1990–1991 came from rejecting the 500 Days Plan and from confiscation.

modelPlan.counter: Judt argues the failure was built into any reform of a command economy, so the reforms could not have made things better quickly.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Was the economy in 1991 worse because of what Gorbachev did? Yes, because shortage and inflation followed his measures directly; the inheritance explains why reform was needed, not why it failed.

segments.text: Gorbachev's reforms did make the Soviet economy worse, because they destroyed the old coordination before a market existed.
In 1988–89 he ordered party committees to stop interfering in the economy and cut ministry staffs, and by 1990 enterprises traded by barter while citizens queued with ration coupons.
This meant that neither plan nor market allocated goods, so supply chains broke down.
However, Judt shows the economy was already shrinking when Gorbachev took over, so the reforms worsened a decline they did not start.
The claim is therefore largely valid: the reforms turned decline into collapse.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the successes and failures of Gorbachev's economic reforms between 1985 and 1991.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: Which outweighed the other, by a stated criterion

modelPlan.thesis: The failures clearly outweighed the successes: legal private enterprise and a real market programme were achievements, but shortage, inflation and the loss of control over the economy decided the outcome.

arguments.claim: Success: cooperatives and private work became legal.
Success: the debate produced a full market programme in 1990.
Failure: shortage and inflation from 1988.
Failure: the centre lost control of the economy to the republics.

modelPlan.counter: The successes laid foundations for post-Soviet reform, so judged in the long term they matter more.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judged by whether living standards and growth improved between 1985 and 1991, the reforms failed.

segments.text: The failures of Gorbachev's economic reforms outweighed their successes.
The cooperatives employed about 150,000 people by the end of 1987, yet by September 1988 staples were missing in Moscow.
This meant that small gains in private services were swamped by the shortages that partial reform created in the state sector.
However, the reforms legalised private enterprise and produced the 500 Days Plan, whose spirit, Campbell notes, shaped later Russian reform.
Judged by growth and living standards in 1985–1991, the reforms therefore failed.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the anti-alcohol campaign and the Law on Cooperatives as attempts at economic reform between 1985 and 1988.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The anti-alcohol campaign and the Law on Cooperatives
decodeKey.scope: Economic reform in the Soviet Union
decodeKey.judgement: Which differences reveal how perestroika changed

modelPlan.thesis: Both reforms tried to raise productivity and both produced unintended costs, but they differed fundamentally in method: the campaign used state compulsion, the cooperatives used private initiative.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both aimed to improve productivity and services.
Similarity: both produced unintended costs, crime and resentment.
Difference: compulsion from above against initiative from below.
Difference: one was abandoned after 1987, the other was extended in 1988.

modelPlan.counter: The similarity in results may matter more than the difference in method: both showed that the state could not control the effects of its own reforms.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference shows perestroika changing? The shift from compulsion to initiative, which marks the move from improving the old system to reforming it.

segments.text: The anti-alcohol campaign and the cooperatives both aimed to raise productivity, but they used opposite methods.
The campaign of May 1985 closed distilleries and restricted sales, whereas the Law on Cooperatives of May 1988 put profit-making cooperatives on the same basis as state enterprises.
This meant that perestroika moved from compelling people to behave differently to allowing them to profit from initiative.
However, both produced unintended costs: moonshine and lost revenue in one case, resentment and protection rackets in the other.
The contrast in method therefore shows how far perestroika had moved by 1988, while the similarity in results shows its limits.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the impact of the Law on State Enterprise on the Soviet economy between 1988 and 1991.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: How far the law, compared with other measures, shaped the crisis

modelPlan.thesis: The law was a major accelerant of the crisis because it freed wages without freeing prices, but its effects combined with money printing, the withdrawal of the party and the republics' actions.

arguments.claim: Wage rises, money printing and empty shops (named factor first).
Judt's dilemma: freedom without a market meant more shortage.
The withdrawal of the party removed the remaining coordination.
By 1990–1991 the republics and the miners took economic authority from the centre.

modelPlan.counter: Campbell calls the law 'tinkering', which suggests its direct impact was smaller than the political decisions that followed.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How much of the crisis would have happened without it? Much less shortage in 1988, so its impact was large, though not sole.

segments.text: The Law on State Enterprise accelerated the crisis because it freed wages without freeing prices.
After it came into effect in January 1988, workers demanded steep wage rises, the government printed money, and by September staples were missing even in Moscow.
This meant that more money chased goods still sold at fixed prices, so goods disappeared into speculation.
However, the free fall of 1989–1990 owed as much to the withdrawal of the party from the economy as to the law itself.
The law's impact was therefore large but not decisive on its own.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons why Gorbachev rejected the 500 Days Plan in 1990.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its reasons and show how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: Gorbachev rejected the plan mainly because it would have transferred economic sovereignty to the republics; fear of the social cost of price rises and conservative pressure reinforced his choice.

arguments.claim: The plan would hand resources and taxes to the republics.
Ryzhkov's bread-price panic showed the social risk of rapid price rises.
The Union parliament preferred decree powers and a compromise.
Russia's adoption of the plan made it a weapon of Yeltsin's against the centre.

modelPlan.counter: Gorbachev did not reject the plan outright: the Basic Guidelines kept its stages, so the difference was about the timetable.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason, if removed, would most likely have changed his decision? The transfer of sovereignty: Seventeen Moments concludes the compromise meant the Union would keep the Union's property.

segments.text: Gorbachev rejected the 500 Days Plan mainly because it would have transferred economic sovereignty to the republics.
The plan passed control of resources and taxes to the republics, and the Russian Supreme Soviet adopted it on 11 September 1990.
This meant that accepting it would have reduced the Union to whatever powers the republics chose to delegate, which Campbell argues Gorbachev was not ready to accept.
However, the October 'Basic Guidelines' kept the plan's four stages, so Gorbachev rejected its timetable and federalism rather than the market itself.
The decisive reason was therefore political: the Union would keep the Union's property.
